extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, district and appellate judges, law clerks, and expert witnesses in patent cases
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural/evidentiary rules applied by the Federal Circuit in reviewing a district-court patent case on summary judgment, collateral estoppel, claim construction, Daubert challenges, and expert admissibility. Focuses on when collateral estoppel and expert exclusions are appropriate and how claim scope should be determined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary judgment standard (Rule 56)
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary judgment is appropriate when 'there is no genuine dispute as to any material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply regional-circuit law for review; in the Eleventh Circuit review is de novo, 'construing the facts and drawing all reasonable inferences in favor of the non-moving party.' A genuine dispute of material fact exists when the evidence is such that a reasonable jury could return a verdict for the nonmoving party. (Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(a); Eleventh Circuit authority quoted.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate review of evidentiary rulings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Eleventh Circuit reviews a district court’s evidentiary rulings for abuse of discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A district court abuses its discretion where its decision rests upon a clearly erroneous finding of fact, an errant conclusion of law, or an improper application of law to fact. Apply regional-circuit standards when reviewing procedural and evidentiary questions, subject to deference where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collateral estoppel / issue preclusion elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Collateral estoppel applies where four elements are satisfied: (1) the issue at stake is identical to the one in the prior litigation; (2) the issue was actually litigated in the prior suit; (3) the determination of the issue in the prior litigation was a critical and necessary part of the judgment; and (4) the party against whom the earlier decision is asserted had a full and fair opportunity to litigate the issue in the earlier proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the Eleventh Circuit’s four requirements (and essentially the same under Federal Circuit law). In patent cases, apply Federal Circuit law to substantive patent issues and to questions where patent-law-specific application of collateral estoppel is implicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply Federal Circuit law to patent-substantive issues
rubrics_metrics.description: When questions involve substantive patent law (e.g., whether a particular claim is the same as or separate from another claim), the Federal Circuit's law governs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although regional-circuit law governs certain procedural questions (like collateral-estoppel procedure), the court applies its own law to substantive patent issues, such as determining whether claims are identical for preclusion purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction process (Phillips/Vitronics)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper approach to determining claim scope is to look first to the intrinsic evidence: the patent itself (claims and specification) and, if in evidence, the prosecution history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extrinsic evidence (expert testimony, dictionaries, treatises) is less significant than the intrinsic record. Extrinsic evidence may not be used to contradict claim meaning that is unambiguous in light of the intrinsic evidence. Claim construction is ultimately a legal question subject to de novo review on appeal, but subsidiary fact-finding for claim construction is for the trial court to perform (Teva).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and limits of extrinsic evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Extrinsic evidence (expert testimony, inventor testimony, dictionaries, treatises) is less significant than intrinsic evidence and cannot be used to contradict an unambiguous claim meaning from the intrinsic record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts should not rely primarily on extrinsic evidence to define claim scope if intrinsic evidence is dispositive. Treat extrinsic materials as subordinate and use them only to aid construction where intrinsic evidence leaves genuine ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collateral estoppel and IPR findings — affirmed invalidity is preclusive
rubrics_metrics.description: An affirmance of an invalidity finding (whether from a district court or the Board) has collateral estoppel effect on all pending or co-pending actions: once a claim has been affirmed invalid, the claim no longer exists and cannot be asserted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite XY, LLC v. Trans Ova Genetics: affirmed invalidity in any forum is preclusive as to that claim across actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on preclusion from PTAB findings where legal standards differ
rubrics_metrics.description: Findings underlying an IPR (which applied a preponderance standard) do not necessarily estop a patentee from defending validity of separate claims in district court where the district court requires proof by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collateral estoppel does not apply where the second action involves a different legal standard (B & B Hardware; Grogan). Because IPR uses preponderance while district court requires clear and convincing, factual findings about prior art capabilities in an IPR do not automatically preclude argument or evidence in district court on different claims that were not adjudicated as invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof differences: IPR vs district court
rubrics_metrics.description: In an IPR, the petitioner must prove unpatentability by a preponderance of the evidence; in district court, a defendant asserting invalidity must prove it by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the burdens differ, Board findings under the lower standard do not necessarily satisfy the higher district-court standard for separate, unadjudicated claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to allow district-court consideration of evidence after IPR
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that were not found unpatentable in the IPR remain presumptively valid and the patentee may present evidence in district court to defend validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts should not preclude patentee’s validity experts from testifying about what the prior art does or does not disclose for claims that survived IPR invalidity challenges; doing so may be legal error where the IPR did not invalidate those claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert admissibility standard — 'appropriate validation' (Doak / Rule 702/703)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed expert testimony must be supported by appropriate validation — 'good grounds, based on what is known.' Under Rule 703 an expert can base opinions on facts or data in the case 'that the expert has been made aware of.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reliance on others’ scientific test results or on documents (schematics, technical documents, design reviews) may be reasonable grounds. Challenges to the bases of expert opinions generally affect weight, not admissibility; district courts should be cautious about excluding testimony solely because the expert did not personally run tests or simulations if other reliable bases were available.

rubrics_metrics.name: When lack of testing/simulation affects admissibility vs weight
rubrics_metrics.description: An expert’s failure to perform independent testing or simulation does not automatically render the testimony inadmissible if the expert reasonably relied on technical documents, schematics, or existing simulation results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts should generally leave disputes about testing and methodology to jurors (weight/credibility). Exclusion is proper only if the expert’s methodology lacks any appropriate validation or is otherwise unreliable as a matter of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of inconsistent expert statements and depositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Inconsistent testimony (e.g., deposition statements that appear to admit a point and later expert declarations that contradict it) can create issues of credibility and may produce genuine disputes of material fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should consider the totality of the record in the light most favorable to the nonmovant; conflicting statements may prevent summary judgment because they allow a reasonable juror to credit one version over another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim scope identity test for collateral estoppel in patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: For collateral estoppel to bar relitigation of infringement, the scope of the claims in the new action must be materially the same as the claims adjudicated previously; differences that materially alter the infringement question defeat preclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination requires claim construction per Phillips; the district court should perform claim construction (looking first to intrinsic evidence) rather than relying primarily on extrinsic expert charts. If claim scope is unresolved or disputed, summary judgment on collateral estoppel is inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction and appellate discretion to resolve issues important on remand
rubrics_metrics.description: Although appellate jurisdiction is generally limited to final decisions, an appellate court may exercise discretion to review non-final or unresolved issues that are likely to be important on remand in the interest of judicial economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where vacation of summary judgment will lead to further proceedings likely involving the issue, the appellate court may address evidentiary rulings (e.g., exclusion of experts) to guide the district court on remand.
